paragraphs: The paper studies a shared decision-making problem in which multiple agents learn through repeated interactions with their environments. Rewards follow a contextual linear bandit model, and a central server helps agents cooperate. The practical challenge is allowing each agent to communicate on its own schedule without forcing the others to communicate too.

The proposed algorithm, FedLinUCB, uses optimism: decisions account for the possibility that uncertain choices could be rewarding. Its defining feature is fully asynchronous communication. An exchange between one agent and the server does not trigger exchanges involving other agents, so cooperation does not require synchronized communication rounds.

The authors prove a regret bound that scales with the context dimension times the square root of the total interactions across agents, up to logarithmic factors. Regret measures the accumulated cost of imperfect decisions while learning. Communication complexity scales with the dimension and the square of the number of agents, again up to logarithmic factors. The result matches the stated single-agent regret guarantee while permitting independent communication schedules.
neurips-2022-a-simple-and-provably-effic.tldr: FedLinUCB enables fully asynchronous federated linear bandit learning with a proven regret guarantee matching the single-agent setting.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains a model on a sequence of tasks, creating the risk that new learning will erase earlier capabilities. The paper focuses on why class incremental learning remains difficult even when methods can effectively address forgetting in task incremental learning. It seeks a theoretical account of the capabilities needed for successful class incremental prediction.

The analysis decomposes class incremental learning probabilistically into prediction within a task and prediction of the task identity. It then establishes a connection between task identity prediction and out-of-distribution detection. This connects recognizing which task an input belongs to with recognizing whether it falls outside a task's distribution.

The central theoretical conclusion is that good within-task prediction together with good task identity prediction, or the associated out-of-distribution detection capability, is necessary and sufficient for good class incremental performance. These capabilities can be implicit in an algorithm. Task incremental learning corresponds to the within-task component. Guided by this result, the authors design methods that substantially outperform strong baselines in both settings.
neurips-2022-a-theoretical-study-on-solv.tldr: The paper connects successful class incremental learning to both within-task prediction and identifying the relevant task through out-of-distribution detection.

paragraphs: Textual backdoor attacks alter training so that predefined triggers can steer a language model's predictions. This paper argues that evaluating such attacks requires attention to how the attacker supplies the compromised material. Releasing a poisoned dataset, a pretrained model, or a fine-tuned model creates different constraints and concerns.

The authors organize evaluation around those three scenarios and broaden what counts as a successful poisoned example. Changing a prediction while preserving ordinary performance does not establish that an attack is unobtrusive or preserves meaning. Their proposed measures include increases in grammar errors and differences in perplexity for stealthiness, alongside text similarity for semantic validity.

The paper implements this evaluation framework in OpenBackdoor, an open-source toolkit used to benchmark attack and defense methods through extensive experiments. It also introduces CUBE, a clustering-based defense baseline aimed at poisoned datasets, an area the authors describe as underexplored. The contribution is a more explicit basis for comparing methods across realistic attack settings and multiple properties of poisoned text.
neurips-2022-a-unified-evaluation-of-tex.tldr: The paper introduces scenario-specific textual backdoor evaluations, broader poisoning metrics, the OpenBackdoor toolkit, and a clustering-based defense.

paragraphs: The paper examines how to explain a Transformer's output using information inside the model. It identifies weaknesses in explanations based primarily on attention weights or individual feature gradients. Attention weights omit the magnitudes of the values being combined, while feature-by-feature gradient attribution can miss interactions that influence the final prediction.

A further concern is the role of skip connections, which carry a substantial portion of information through Transformers. Explanations centered on self-attention may leave this information flow insufficiently represented. Together, these observations motivate an explanation method that draws on several signals instead of treating one internal quantity as a complete account.

AttCAT combines encoded features, their gradients, and their attention weights to produce attentive class activation tokens. The intended result is a more faithful explanation of the model's output. Extensive experiments report superior performance over baseline methods across different Transformer architectures, evaluation metrics, datasets, and tasks. These findings support the usefulness of the combined signals across the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-attcat-explaining-transform.tldr: AttCAT combines Transformer features, gradients, and attention weights to improve explanations across the evaluated architectures and tasks.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from a teacher network to a student. This paper investigates doing so using only random Gaussian samples, eliminating the need to supply the teacher's original training data during distillation. That possibility matters when access to training examples is restricted or raises privacy concerns.

The authors identify a specific obstacle: Gaussian inputs produce hidden-layer activation distributions that differ from those produced by the teacher's familiar training data. They describe this shift as the key factor limiting the consistency of previous noise-based approaches. Their method applies a simple correction intended to reduce the mismatch inside the teacher network.

Experiments on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, SVHN, and Food101 show that Gaussian samples alone can support student performance close to the teacher on vision tasks such as classification. The authors also report that, when only a small amount of original data is available, their noise-based method can substantially outperform distillation using that available data. These findings establish the potential of addressing internal activation mismatch for data-free transfer.
neurips-2022-discovering-and-overcoming-.tldr: Reducing hidden-activation distribution shifts enables effective teacher-to-student distillation using Gaussian noise instead of original training data.

paragraphs: The paper studies regression whose design matrix is a tensor product of several smaller matrices. The resulting matrix combines the factors into a much larger structured object. The goal is to fit a label vector, but the factors change over time: at each step, one receives a sparse update.

Recomputing the regression solution after every change is expensive because the full product can be large even when its constituent matrices are manageable. The authors instead maintain a sketch, a compact representation of the tensor product that supports updating the solution. Their central contribution is a dynamic tree data structure that propagates a change to one factor quickly through the tree.

This organization makes the evolving product structure useful for computation rather than requiring a fresh solution at every step. The authors show that the same data structure supports dynamic tensor product regression, tensor product spline regression, and maintenance of low-rank approximations. Its significance is therefore a shared update mechanism for several computations involving changing tensor products.
neurips-2022-dynamic-tensor-product-regr.tldr: A dynamic tree maintains tensor-product sketches so regression solutions and related approximations can be updated efficiently after sparse changes.

paragraphs: Local optimization methods reduce communication in distributed learning by allowing work between exchanges. Much previous analysis established first-order guarantees, which concern small gradients. This paper asks whether a local method can also escape saddle points and obtain second-order guarantees without losing the communication advantages that make local training attractive.

The proposed BVR-L-PSGD algorithm combines a bias-variance reduced gradient estimator with perturbations to the model parameters. The estimator supports the local optimization process, while perturbations enable the saddle-point escape objective. The authors analyze this combination for centralized nonconvex distributed optimization and prove second-order optimality with nearly the communication complexity of the corresponding first-order BVR-L-SGD method.

The communication advantage is qualified by how different the local datasets are. The bound improves over non-local methods when this heterogeneity is smaller than the smoothness of the local loss. As heterogeneity approaches zero, the communication complexity approaches a constant up to logarithmic factors. Numerical results support the theoretical findings, linking stronger optimization guarantees to favorable similarity among local datasets.
neurips-2022-escaping-saddle-points-with.tldr: BVR-L-PSGD adds saddle-point escape guarantees to local distributed optimization with nearly the communication cost of its first-order counterpart.

paragraphs: In a pseudo-game, a player's action can change both other players' payoffs and which strategies they may choose. A generalized Nash equilibrium requires everyone's choice to be feasible and leaves no player able to improve through a feasible unilateral change. Computing such equilibria is hard in general, motivating methods for structured cases.

The paper approaches equilibrium computation by minimizing exploitability, the sum of players' regrets about their current choices. Although this quantity is generally nondifferentiable, the authors reformulate its minimization as a min-max problem. This enables first-order optimization methods that operate through the reformulated objective.

For pseudo-games with convex-concave cumulative regret and jointly convex constraints, the methods compute variational equilibria, a refinement of generalized Nash equilibria, in polynomial time. Under Lipschitz smoothness and jointly convex constraints, they more generally find stationary points of exploitability in polynomial time. Experiments outperform known algorithms and sometimes reach generalized Nash equilibria beyond the guaranteed setting with suitable initialization; this latter outcome is empirical rather than guaranteed.
neurips-2022-exploitability-minimization.tldr: Recasting exploitability minimization as min-max optimization yields polynomial-time first-order guarantees for specified classes of pseudo-games.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection faces two linked problems: abnormalities are difficult to enumerate, and what counts as normal changes between tasks. Learning a separate normal-data distribution for every new task can require substantial data collection and training. This paper develops an approach intended to adapt quickly from only a few examples.

Its energy-based model assigns lower energy to correct values and higher energy to incorrect ones. Langevin dynamics generates incorrect samples through an iterative optimization procedure. This provides a way to train around unfavorable examples without attempting to explicitly model the entire space of possible anomalies.

An adaptive sparse coding layer supplies the mechanism for updating what is normal during inference. The authors train with a meta-learning scheme that simulates adaptation from a few examples, aligning training with the intended deployment behavior. The combination addresses sample generation, rapid adaptation, and limited task-specific data within one approach. The abstract reports strong empirical support for the findings, while framing fast adaptation as the central design objective.
neurips-2022-few-shot-fast-adaptive-anom.tldr: The method combines energy-based learning, adaptive sparse coding, and meta-learning to support anomaly detection that adapts from a few examples.

paragraphs: The paper studies how message passing neural networks generalize in graph classification and regression. Its central question concerns the relationship between model complexity, the number of training graphs, and the size of those graphs. The analysis assumes that graphs belonging to different classes come from different random graph models.

Under this sampling setup, the generalization bound worsens as the neural network becomes more complex and improves as the training set grows. It also improves as the average number of nodes per graph increases. Graph size therefore enters the theoretical account alongside the number of graph examples, helping explain how a complex network can generalize from a small collection of large graphs.

The proof rests on a uniform convergence result connecting a network's output on a sampled graph to its output on the underlying geometric model that the graph discretizes. This connection supplies the basis for the graph-size dependence. The resulting explanation is tied to the assumed random graph setting, rather than asserting that larger graphs always improve generalization.
neurips-2022-generalization-analysis-of-.tldr: Under the paper's random graph assumptions, larger graphs improve generalization bounds for message passing networks alongside larger training sets.

paragraphs: Standard message passing networks repeatedly gather information from immediate neighbors. K-hop methods instead aggregate information from neighborhoods extending several hops at once. This paper asks what additional graph structures that change lets a network distinguish, first separating two K-hop aggregation kernels that earlier work had sometimes conflated.

The theoretical results place K-hop message passing above the 1-WL graph-distinguishing test and show that it can distinguish almost all regular graphs. The improvement has limits: some simple regular graphs remain indistinguishable, and the method's expressiveness is bounded by 3-WL. Reaching farther through a graph therefore increases distinguishing power without resolving every structural ambiguity.

The authors introduce KP-GNN to incorporate peripheral subgraph information at each hop. This additional information enables the framework to distinguish many distance-regular graphs that previous distance encodings or 3-WL methods cannot distinguish. Experiments support its expressive power and effectiveness, with competitive performance across the evaluated benchmarks. The contribution combines a characterization of ordinary K-hop methods with a concrete way to exceed their identified limits.
neurips-2022-how-powerful-are-k-hop-mess.tldr: The paper characterizes K-hop graph networks' expressive limits and introduces KP-GNN to distinguish additional structures using peripheral subgraphs.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an approach to automated theorem proving for settings where training examples are unavailable or difficult to generate. It starts with a generic expert strategy expressed as a nondeterministic program: a high-level procedure that leaves choices open. Learning then refines how those choices are made during search.

An AlphaZero-style learner trains itself to improve that strategy. Alongside it, a teacher agent also self-trains, generating tasks intended to have suitable relevance and difficulty for the learner. Task generation and proof search thus both become learning problems, while the high-level strategy provides a way to incorporate a small amount of domain knowledge.

The authors illustrate the approach with loop invariant synthesis for imperative programs. In this application, neural networks refine both the teacher's strategy and the solver's strategy. The contribution is the combination of structured expert guidance, self-training search, and an adaptive source of tasks. It offers a route to working on proof-related problems without first assembling a conventional collection of training examples.
neurips-2022-learning-to-find-proofs-and.tldr: Self-training teacher and solver agents refine high-level search strategies for theorem proving, illustrated through loop invariant synthesis.

paragraphs: Causal discovery methods often expect complete observations, but practical datasets frequently contain missing values. Filling those gaps with a separate imputation method before discovering causal structure can introduce bias into the modeled data distribution. MissDAG addresses the incomplete observations within the causal discovery procedure itself.

The method primarily assumes ignorable missingness and identifiable additive noise models. It uses expectation-maximization to maximize an expected likelihood based on the visible observations. When the relevant posterior calculations are unavailable in closed form, Monte Carlo expectation-maximization approximates the likelihood, allowing the procedure to continue without requiring an exact analytical expression.

During the maximization step, MissDAG uses the additive noise structure and density transformations to obtain simpler formulations for noise distributions. It then applies likelihood-based causal discovery while enforcing a directed acyclic graph constraint. The framework can incorporate different causal discovery algorithms. Simulations and real-data experiments demonstrate its flexibility and effectiveness, supporting the value of integrating missing-data treatment with causal modeling under the stated assumptions.
neurips-2022-missdag-causal-discovery-in.tldr: MissDAG integrates expectation-maximization with causal discovery to learn from incomplete observations under additive-noise and missingness assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper studies signal recovery when measurements pass a Gaussian projection of the signal through an unknown, possibly random nonlinear function. This allows the measurement relationship to be misspecified. The analysis assumes a nonzero covariance between the observed response and the squared projection, giving the observations a particular statistical connection to the signal.

The signal is also assumed to belong to the range of a Lipschitz-continuous generative model whose inputs are bounded and k-dimensional. This prior describes candidate signals through a lower-dimensional input space. The proposed recovery procedure first forms a spectral initialization, then iteratively refines the resulting estimate.

Under suitable conditions, both stages achieve a statistical rate proportional to the square root of k log L times log m divided by m, where L is the generator's Lipschitz constant and m is the measurement count. Image experiments show performance comparable to or substantially better than several competing methods. The contribution links recovery under an unknown measurement function to a structured generative signal model.
neurips-2022-misspecified-phase-retrieva.tldr: A two-stage method recovers generatively structured signals from misspecified nonlinear measurements with statistical guarantees under stated conditions.

paragraphs: NaturalProver studies mathematical proofs written in the mixture of symbols and ordinary language used by people. The paper considers two tasks: suggesting the next step of a proof and generating a complete proof. Both require connecting the statement being proved to relevant mathematical background.

The model conditions its generation on references such as definitions and theorems, supplied either through retrieval or by a person. An optional constrained decoding procedure enforces the presence of those references in the output. This makes background material an explicit part of proof generation and gives the generation process a way to incorporate selected references.

On NaturalProofs theorems, university-level mathematics students judge NaturalProver's next-step suggestions and complete proofs more favorably than those of fine-tuned GPT-3. The model proves some theorems requiring short proofs of two to six steps, and more than 40% of its next-step suggestions are rated correct and useful. These findings establish partial proof-generation and assistance capabilities in the evaluated setting, with the strongest demonstrated complete proofs remaining short.
neurips-2022-naturalprover-grounded-math.tldr: NaturalProver uses mathematical references to improve human-rated proof suggestions and generate some correct short proofs.

paragraphs: The paper considers a seller offering heterogeneous items to one buyer whose values add across items. Those values follow a known distribution and may be correlated. Earlier results show that mechanisms with bounded menu complexity can capture an arbitrarily small fraction of optimal revenue for some distributions.

The authors reverse the usual question: what must a distribution look like if it produces such an infinite separation? A known construction starts from a sequence of vectors with a geometric property and produces a qualifying value distribution. The first main result shows that this construction is comprehensive: every distribution witnessing an infinite separation could arise through that framework.

The second result examines an earlier, more restrictive construction and proves that it is not comprehensive. The authors provide a distribution with an infinite gap that cannot arise from the restrictive framework. As a consequence, they identify a new kind of mechanism that witnesses infinite separations on instances where earlier aligned mechanisms do not. The findings clarify both the reach and the boundaries of existing geometric constructions.
neurips-2022-on-infinite-separations-bet.tldr: The paper characterizes the scope of constructions producing infinite revenue gaps between simple and optimal selling mechanisms.

paragraphs: The paper learns individual preferences from comparisons in which users choose between items represented by feature vectors. Its model combines a shared distance metric, describing the crowd's general notion of item similarity, with a separate latent ideal point for each user. This allows common structure and personal preferences to be learned together.

Sharing the metric means that the data needed to learn it can be distributed across respondents. The authors first study an idealized setting with noiseless continuous responses expressing differences in item distances. That analysis addresses fundamental learning limits before moving to noisy binary comparisons of the kind people can provide.

For binary measurements, the paper establishes prediction-error guarantees and shows improved sample complexity when the shared metric is low-rank. It also provides recovery guarantees under assumptions on the response distribution. Experiments use simulated data and a large collection of users' color preferences. The contribution is a joint model with theoretical support for pooling information while retaining a representation of each person's preferences.
neurips-2022-one-for-all-simultaneous-me.tldr: A shared similarity metric and individual ideal points allow preference learning to pool information across users with prediction and recovery guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies pricing for services that occupy a sequence of reusable resources. Customers arrive randomly, and serving one product can involve several resources in the network. The firm must choose prices to maximize expected revenue while initially lacking knowledge of how each product's demand responds to price.

The authors develop batched bandit learning algorithms that learn near-optimal pricing policies through interaction. Their cumulative regret guarantee is near-optimal and scales as the number of products times the square root of the number of candidate prices multiplied by the number of service periods, up to logarithmic factors. Regret captures the revenue cost of learning while making pricing decisions.

A key part of the analysis concerns how an open queueing network evolves over finite time. The paper provides what the authors describe as the first finite-time mixing analysis for a Jackson network, supporting the pricing guarantee and potentially serving other queueing analyses. Numerical studies report consistently good performance for the proposed approaches, complementing the theoretical account of learning with reusable resources.
neurips-2022-online-learning-and-pricing.tldr: Batched bandit algorithms learn service prices with near-optimal regret when customers use networks of reusable resources.

paragraphs: Intrinsic rewards encourage a reinforcement learning agent to visit novel states. They can help when ordinary exploration rarely reaches useful task rewards, but can also keep an agent exploring after the task already supplies enough guidance. This creates a balancing problem: curiosity may help on one task and distract from success on another.

The paper introduces Extrinsic-Intrinsic Policy Optimization, or EIPO, as a constrained optimization procedure for adjusting that balance automatically. It reduces the importance of intrinsic reward when exploration is unnecessary and increases it when exploration is needed. The aim is to preserve useful exploration without requiring manual tuning of its weight against task reward.

The authors report consistent performance gains across sixty-one Atari games. This evaluation supports the claim that adjusting curiosity through the proposed optimization procedure can work across tasks with differing exploration demands. The contribution concerns how intrinsic and task rewards are balanced during learning, addressing the inconsistent performance that can arise when curiosity continues to drive behavior despite available task rewards.
neurips-2022-redeeming-intrinsic-rewards.tldr: EIPO automatically adjusts intrinsic reward through constrained optimization, with reported performance gains across sixty-one Atari games.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns semantic categories across an image. SegViT explores how a plain Vision Transformer can support this task by generating segmentation masks through attention. The central design uses relationships between class representations and spatial image features as the basis for deciding where each class appears.

Its Attention-to-Mask module compares a set of learnable class tokens with spatial feature maps and converts the resulting similarity maps into segmentation masks. This gives attention a direct role in constructing the output. Experiments show improvements over other plain-ViT segmentation models on ADE20K and report new state-of-the-art results on COCO-Stuff-10K and PASCAL-Context.

The paper also addresses the computational expense of the Transformer backbone. Query-based down-sampling and up-sampling form a Shrunk structure that reduces the computation required by the model. The authors report savings of up to 40% while maintaining competitive performance. Together, the mask-generation module and the reduced-computation structure demonstrate both segmentation capability and a way to make the backbone less expensive in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-segvit-semantic-segmentatio.tldr: SegViT turns class-token attention into segmentation masks and introduces a structure that saves up to 40% of computation while remaining competitive.

paragraphs: The paper studies smoothed online convex optimization, where a learner makes decisions over time and pays two kinds of costs: the cost associated with each decision and the cost of changing decisions. This makes adaptation a balancing problem. Moving toward a better decision can help with the current objective while also adding a switching cost.

The authors build a simple algorithm by combining versions of online gradient descent that use different step sizes. Step size controls how far a gradient update moves the decision. Their method combines these versions sequentially using a prediction strategy called Discounted-Normal-Predictor. The approach is motivated by earlier guarantees for that strategy in learning with expert advice when switching also carries a cost.

The main result is a proof of nearly optimal adaptive regret with switching costs on every interval. Thus, the guarantee concerns performance within individual stretches of the decision sequence, rather than only an aggregate over the whole sequence. Using an existing dynamic-regret guarantee for online gradient descent, the authors also establish control of dynamic regret with switching costs on every interval, extending the analysis to comparisons with decisions that can change over time.
neurips-2022-smoothed-online-convex-opti.tldr: The paper combines online gradient descent methods through Discounted-Normal-Predictor to obtain nearly optimal adaptive regret and control dynamic regret on every interval while accounting for switching costs.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes online value-based reinforcement learning with neural networks and epsilon-greedy exploration, a setting motivated by deep Q-networks. It asks how network width, depth, and the mathematical class of the value function affect learning guarantees beyond a linear approximation regime. The target is an alpha-smooth Q-function in a d-dimensional feature space.

For deep networks associated with Besov function spaces, the authors give sufficient scaling conditions for sublinear regret: width grows roughly as T raised to d divided by 2 alpha plus d, and depth grows logarithmically with the number of episodes T. For two-layer networks associated with Barron space, width scaling of order at least the square root of T is sufficient.

The technical challenge is that epsilon-greedy exploration does not itself ensure optimism. The analysis instead expresses temporal-difference error in an integrated squared-error space under an averaged measure, turning its estimation into a generalization problem with dependent data. These are sufficient architecture conditions within the analyzed function spaces, rather than necessary network sizes for every reinforcement learning problem.
neurips-2022-understanding-deep-neural-f.tldr: The paper gives sufficient neural-network size conditions for sublinear regret in online reinforcement learning with epsilon-greedy exploration.

paragraphs: Inverse problems reconstruct signals from measurements that may omit part of the original information. When training uses one fixed incomplete measurement process, learning is impossible in general because some signal directions never affect the observations. Using several measurement operators can overcome this obstacle, but requires understanding when their combined information is sufficient.

The paper establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for learning the underlying signal model used for reconstruction. These conditions connect the number of distinct operators, measurements per operator, signal-model dimension, and ambient signal dimension. The contribution explains how these quantities interact rather than treating measurement diversity alone as an unconditional solution.

The authors also propose an unsupervised loss that needs only incomplete measurements. They report performance comparable to supervised learning when the sufficient condition is satisfied. Experiments on accelerated magnetic resonance imaging, compressed sensing, and image inpainting validate the theoretical bounds and demonstrate advantages over previous methods. The findings connect an information-based account of learnability to a concrete reconstruction-training objective.
neurips-2022-unsupervised-learning-from-.tldr: The paper characterizes when multiple incomplete measurement operators enable learning and proposes an unsupervised reconstruction loss supported by those conditions.

paragraphs: Collaborative perception lets agents share complementary observations, but sending more information consumes bandwidth. Where2comm addresses this tradeoff by asking which spatial regions are most useful to communicate. Its spatial confidence map represents differences in perceptual information across locations, allowing communication to focus on a sparse set of important regions.

The framework uses these maps to select perceptually critical information and supports practical compression. It can also adjust the spatial areas involved in communication as available bandwidth changes. This makes the amount and location of transmitted information responsive to the communication budget while preserving the goal of improving perception.

The authors evaluate 3D object detection in real and simulated settings involving cameras, LiDAR, cars, and drones across four datasets. They report consistent improvements over previous methods. On OPV2V, one highlighted result uses more than 100,000 times less communication volume while outperforming DiscoNet and V2X-ViT. That comparison illustrates the potential of spatial selection in the evaluated setting, rather than a universal reduction for every deployment.
neurips-2022-where2comm-communication-ef.tldr: Where2comm uses spatial confidence maps to share critical regions, improving evaluated collaborative perception while sharply reducing communication.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection aims to identify inputs outside a model's familiar domain. This paper reexamines defenses against adversarial manipulation using end-to-end PGD attacks on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution data. With larger perturbations, including sizes up to 8/255 on CIFAR-10, almost all evaluated defenses perform worse than random detection.

The proposed Adversarially Trained Discriminator combines a pretrained robust feature extractor with a generator that supplies out-of-distribution samples. Its training uses both familiar examples and outliers to address attacks on either side of the detection decision. For stability, the authors adversarially perturb real in-distribution examples and real outliers, while leaving generated outliers unattacked during discriminator training.

With CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 as the in-distribution datasets, ATD substantially improves robust AUROC over previous methods while maintaining high standard AUROC and classification accuracy. The findings show that ordinary detection performance can coexist with severe adversarial weakness, and support the proposed training choices in the evaluated settings. They do not establish that access to outliers is universally necessary.
neurips-2022-your-out-of-distribution-de.tldr: Stronger attacks expose weaknesses in evaluated OOD defenses, while ATD improves robust detection using robust features and adversarial discriminator training.
